videoIdeas.title: 5 things nobody tells you about leading at 20
videoIdeas.hook: Nobody hands you leadership. You take it before you feel ready.
videoIdeas.rationale: Daanish's 'if you're in your 20s pls save this' listicle series is doing 60k+ views on repeat, and birdtart's career listicles hit millions. You don't have a single saveable leadership listicle yet — and your top post ever was literally about a leadership programme. This is your lane, untapped in this format.
videoIdeas.script:
Nobody hands you leadership. You take it before you feel ready. Here are 5 things nobody tells you.

One. The person running the room is usually just the one who stopped waiting to be picked. That's it. They volunteered first.

Two. Your team doesn't need you to have the answer. They need you to decide. Indecision kills more projects than bad decisions ever will.

Three. You will be the youngest in the room for years. Stop apologising for it. Being underestimated is an advantage — use it.

Four. Praise in public, correct in private. Break that rule once and you lose the room for good.

Five. Leadership isn't a title. It's whether people would follow you if you had no title at all. Build that. Save this.

visuals.setting: Walking shot through a university campus or community centre corridor, smart-casual — shirt, no blazer. Confident pace, talking directly to camera. Natural daylight.
visuals.visualHook: On-screen text '5 things nobody tells you about leading at 20' slams in on the first frame while you're mid-stride, then a hard cut to your face as you deliver the first line.
otherHookIdeas: Cold open mid-walk pointing at camera: 'You — stop waiting to be picked.'
On-screen counter 1/5...5/5 ticking in the corner to drive saves and rewatches
Open on an empty chair at the head of a table, then you sit in it as the hook lands

videoIdeas.title: How to not freeze when everyone's looking at you
videoIdeas.hook: The fear doesn't go away. You just get better at talking through it.
videoIdeas.rationale: Public speaking is one of your three pillars but barely appears in your top posts. Practical, teachable 'how to' content performs (Daanish's journaling, birdtart's networking questions). This fills a pillar gap with a save-worthy skill video.
videoIdeas.script:
The fear doesn't go away. You just get better at talking through it. Let me save you ten years of embarrassment.

When you freeze, it's not because you forgot your words. It's because your brain decided everyone's judging you. They're not. They're thinking about themselves.

So do three things.

First — slow down. When you panic you speed up, and speed sounds like fear. Pause. A pause feels like forever to you and powerful to them.

Second — talk to one person, not the crowd. Pick a face. Finish a thought. Move to the next face. Suddenly it's a conversation, not a performance.

Third — stop trying to be impressive. Try to be clear. Clear always beats clever.

You don't need confidence to start. You start, and the confidence shows up late. It always does.

visuals.setting: Seated or standing at a podium / in front of an empty lecture hall or event space. Blazer or smart shirt. Calm, measured energy — you're modelling the composure you're teaching.
visuals.visualHook: Open on a wide shot of you standing frozen in front of empty seats, dead silent for one beat, then cut close as you say the hook — the silence IS the pattern interrupt.
otherHookIdeas: On-screen text punchline: 'They're not judging you. They forgot you by lunch.'
Cold open mid-pause — hold a 2 second silence before the first word to demonstrate the technique you're teaching
Split moment: show a sped-up nervous clip vs slowed-down calm clip of the same line

videoIdeas.title: The Andalusia mistake we're repeating
videoIdeas.hook: In 711 they welcomed Muslims as liberators. 780 years later they were gone. Here's what killed it.
videoIdeas.rationale: Your Andalusia post (1640 views, no caption-chasing) shows your audience responds to Islamic history tied to a lesson. Dinoo proves faith+reflection content travels. Turn history into a mindset lesson for young Muslims — your distinct edge none of the competitors fully own.
videoIdeas.script:
In 711, Christians were begging Muslims to liberate them. 780 years later, Muslims were gone from Spain entirely. Here's what actually killed Andalusia — and we're doing it again.

It wasn't a single battle. It was decades of division. Taifa kingdoms fighting each other, inviting outside enemies in just to win petty disputes against their own.

They had the knowledge. They had the wealth. They had the civilisation the rest of Europe was copying. What they didn't have was unity.

Sound familiar? We out-argue each other online over things that won't matter in a year while the actual work goes undone.

Andalusia wasn't lost to a stronger enemy. It was lost to a divided self. Learn the lesson or repeat it.

visuals.setting: Film indoors with a bookshelf or plain dark backdrop, serious tone, smart dark top. Slower, deliberate delivery — this is a history lesson, not a hype reel.
visuals.visualHook: Open on a hard date on screen — '711 AD' — then it rapidly ticks forward to '1492' as you say the hook, visualising the fall in one motion.
otherHookIdeas: Cold open on a map of Al-Andalus shrinking as you speak
On-screen text: 'They didn't lose to a stronger enemy.' hold the pause before the reveal
Hold up a book on Andalusian history as a prop, then put it down to deliver

videoIdeas.title: Being in the room beats being the best in the room
videoIdeas.hook: I'm not the fastest runner in the room. But I'm in the room. That's the whole point.
videoIdeas.rationale: Your 'might not be the fastest, but I am in the room' post did 2666 views and 122 likes — strong engagement rate for you. Expand that exact line into a full mindset piece. It's already proven resonance; double down on the format that worked for YOU specifically.
videoIdeas.script:
I'm not the fastest runner in the room. But I'm in the room. And most people never even make it that far.

Everyone's obsessed with being the best. The best speaker, the best student, the smartest in the group chat. And because they're not the best yet, they don't show up at all.

That's the mistake. The gap isn't between good and best. The gap is between showing up and staying home.

The room is full of people who were once worse than you. They just kept turning up until they belonged there.

You don't earn your place by being the best on day one. You earn it by being there on day one — and every day after.

Be in the room. The skill comes later.

visuals.setting: Film at a running track, gym, or event you actually attended — real environment, sportswear or event clothes. Authentic, slightly out of breath energy works here.
visuals.visualHook: Cold open mid-run or walking into a crowded room, camera following behind you, on-screen text: 'Not the best here. Still here.'
otherHookIdeas: Pattern interrupt: start in last place in a group, then the text flips the framing
Point the camera at the room/crowd first, then back to yourself for the line
On-screen text punchline at the end: 'Showing up is the skill'

videoIdeas.title: How to speak so people actually listen
videoIdeas.hook: You don't have a confidence problem. You have a clarity problem.
videoIdeas.rationale: birdtart's practical 'here's exactly what to say' networking video hit 2M views — the niche rewards concrete, scriptable communication tips. You have zero of these in your top posts despite public speaking being a core pillar. Direct, actionable, high save potential.
videoIdeas.script:
You don't have a confidence problem. You have a clarity problem. Fix the second and the first fixes itself.

When people don't listen to you, it's rarely because you're quiet. It's because you bury the point.

Stop opening with 'so, basically, I just wanted to kind of say...' — you've lost them before you've started.

Lead with the conclusion. Say the thing first, explain it second. 'We should move the event to Saturday. Here's why.' Done. People lean in.

Cut the filler words. Every 'um' and 'like' tells the room you're not sure. Silence is better than filler. Silence sounds like you're thinking. Filler sounds like you're stalling.

And slow down. Nobody important rushes. The person who speaks slowly is the person who assumes they'll be listened to. Become that person.

visuals.setting: Clean, direct piece-to-camera. Smart shirt, plain backdrop, well-lit. Sharp and composed — you embody the clarity you're preaching. Slightly closer framing for intimacy.
visuals.visualHook: On-screen text drops the reframe instantly: 'Not a confidence problem → a clarity problem' with a visual arrow, while you deliver the line deadpan.
otherHookIdeas: Cold open with the bad version — mumble 'so basically I just kind of wanted to...' then cut sharply and sit up: 'Stop. Do this instead.'
On-screen filler-word counter that ticks up then slashes to zero
Deliver the first line, pause 2 seconds in silence to demonstrate the point

videoIdeas.title: The cold message that actually gets a reply
videoIdeas.hook: Stop sending 'hey, hope you're well' to people you want to learn from. Here's what to send instead.
videoIdeas.rationale: birdtart's cold email and networking videos are her biggest hits (180k–2M views). This format — specific, copy-this scripts for reaching out — is proven in the niche and completely absent from your account. Ties to leadership/opportunity-building for young Muslims.
videoIdeas.script:
Stop sending 'hey, hope you're well' to people you want to learn from. They get fifty of those a week and ignore all of them. Here's what actually gets a reply.

Three rules.

One. Be specific about them. Not 'I love your work.' Say 'Your point about X changed how I approached Y.' Specific proves you're real, not spraying the same message to a hundred people.

Two. Make the ask tiny. Don't ask for a mentor. Don't ask for a coffee they have to travel for. Ask one question they can answer in two lines. Small asks get answered. Big asks get left on read.

Three. Make it easy to say no. 'No worries if you're busy' outperforms pressure every time. People help when they don't feel cornered.

The people you look up to are more reachable than you think. You're just messaging them like everyone else. Don't.

visuals.setting: Film with a phone in hand, or sitting at a desk with a laptop — show the actual act of typing a message. Smart-casual, focused energy. Could overlay a mock message on screen.
visuals.visualHook: Screen-record a phone typing 'hey, hope you're well' then a big red X slashes across it as you say the hook.
otherHookIdeas: On-screen text shows a 'Seen' / left-on-read notification as the pattern interrupt
Split screen: the bad message vs the good message side by side
Deliver straight to camera holding your phone up, then flip to show the template on screen

postSuggestions.whatsWorking: This is your top post at 4761 views — proof your audience actively wants leadership content tied to a concrete programme/opportunity. The specificity (MCB Visionary Leadership Programme, real activities listed) gives people a reason to care and share. Leadership is clearly your highest-ceiling pillar.
postSuggestions.whatToImprove: The caption opens with a logistics question ('What do you do on the...') rather than a hook that pulls a scroller in. Only 8 comments on 4761 views means it informed but didn't provoke. End with a direct ask — 'Tag someone who should apply' or 'Would you lead a campaign in your city? Yes or no' — to convert views into comments and shares.

postSuggestions.whatsWorking: Your highest engagement rate post — 122 likes and 12 comments on 2666 views. The line 'Might not be the fastest in the room. But I am in the room' is your voice at its best: blunt, articulate, a real idea in one breath. This is the template to replicate (see video idea 4).
postSuggestions.whatToImprove: You left the idea in the caption and let the hashtags do the work. This deserved to be the spoken hook of a full mindset video, not a throwaway line under a running clip. Reuse this exact sentence as an on-screen hook and build 30 seconds around it — you're sitting on a proven angle.

postSuggestions.whatsWorking: 1640 views with zero caption-bait shows your Islamic history content travels on substance alone. The Andalusia narrative is distinctive — none of your competitors own the 'history as a lesson for young Muslims' lane the way you can. Strong differentiator.
postSuggestions.whatToImprove: 33 likes and 0 comments means it was watched but didn't land a takeaway people wanted to react to. History without a sharp present-day lesson is just a story. Close every historical video with one blunt line connecting it to the viewer's life today (e.g. 'lost to a divided self — sound familiar?') and ask a question to force engagement.

postSuggestions.whatsWorking: Opening with 'Burnout affects so many of us' names a real pain point your student-age audience feels — that's the right instinct. The topic (mindset + mental health) aligns with what's working for Dinoo ('you can pray and still need help' did 48k).
postSuggestions.whatToImprove: At 701 views this is your weakest top post, and it reads like an app promo, not a Shawon take. It leads with the problem then pivots to a product. Lead with your own blunt opinion on burnout first, earn the attention, and mention the tool only at the very end — or drop the promo framing entirely and make it a pure mindset piece.

postSuggestions.whatsWorking: 289 likes — your most-liked post, driven by conviction and a well-placed hadith. It proves your audience rallies hard behind principled, speak-up-for-justice content. The Prophetic quote gives it weight and shareability, and the moral clarity is exactly your 'sharp older brother' voice.
postSuggestions.whatToImprove: It's a Sidecar (carousel) with only 1 comment — high likes, almost no conversation. Justice content like this should drive discussion and action, not just a like. Add a clear call to action (what should people actually DO — sign, share, attend) and consider a video version, since every other high performer in your niche and competitors' is video, not static.
